If a wounded person overcomes that obstacle, are they brave, or tough? What about a cancer patient?

Is it tough or brave to fight someone bigger and stronger? It's almost never wise. Maybe you are brave for trying but tough if you win.

I'm curious about the venn diagram of toughness and bravery and where they do and don't overlap.
Do we often mistake courage for toughness? How are they interrelated? Is fear a bigger driver of toughness?

Something can be incredibly tough yet not require much bravery.

For example a pro powerlifter can lift 50 kg's under his maximum weight and still be considered extremely tough. However he would not be brave as little to no risk is involved. Same goes for a man that participates in the Kennedy march and walks 80 kilometers. Most certainly relatively tough but there is no real risk.

You can be tough without facing severe risks but bravery nearly always requires an element of risk.

So my answer would be.

  • Wounded person: Both
  • Cancer patient: Both (tough in body and spirit and brave in standing firm against the threat of death without giving ground.)
  • Weaker man losing vs stronger man: brave
  • Weaker man winning vs stronger man: both
  • Stronger man winning vs another relatively strong man: primarily tough
I can't disagree with you. Risk seems to be the essential element. I suppose the risk for the cancer patient is the pain and nebulous outcome, when suicide is the unspoken option.

Pretty much.

Heck fighting against anything that threatens to maim/kill you requires some level of bravery. More dangerous then suicide for most people in such situations is despair/hopelessness. It takes bravery to fight at full force when the odds of winning/surviving are against you.

For cancer patients losing hope is basically a slower less frowned upon method of suicide.

Although there is a difference between accepting inevitable death and living the last bit of your life as freely as possible and losing hope which has to be noted.

What exactly is Knowledge Management?

oooh, I probably can talk for hours about it. It's a very interesting field that's been gaining traction in the past 20 years or so. This wiki article gives an accurate (albeit dry) sum-up. Basically establishing a proper knowledge management framework in a company saves tons of money by letting people find the knowledge they need when they need it. The very basic/raw version of it is creating a corporate wiki, but it's much more than that.

That's really cool, thanks.

Pretty sure I have a good idea of what you do now. Must be frustrating at times.
I've got fifteen years of library experience and was thinking about moving into this field. Could you recommend a pathway, degree etc?

Oh, it's a really exciting field to get into and the good news is that more and more companies recognize the need for proper knowledge management (KM). I find it most comfortable to do knowledge management in IT/software companies. One needs to be sort of jack of all trades. The skills/experience that are important (and it's all subjective, just from my experience) are:

  • Project management (milestones, KPIs and all that language)
  • Technical writing (ability to get a piece of information from engineers and rework it to the target audience for easy consumption)
  • Taxonomy experience (this is where you excel, I am sure, with your background)
  • A little bit of analytics (e.g. Google Analytics)
  • Know the current tools on the market (e.g. Atlassian Confluence)
  • A little bit of online marketing
  • At least basic understanding of how support works (you will find that support people are the ones that will help you sell your KM strategy to the management folks the most)
  • Some knowledge of the industry (e.g. 10 years ago when I started around 20% preferred finding information online over contacting a company for help directly; right now around 70% of users google before going for support)

You may want to invest in a KM certificate (e.g. at http://www.kminstitute.org/).

Read the guides by the KCS consortium (http://www.serviceinnovation.org/kcs/). They are really good and up to date.

Buy and read this book: Designing a Successful KM Strategy. It's really worth it.

If you have any questions, I'm happy to help.

Recently, I bought a set of second-hand syphon gears from my good-ol barista mate. Of course, I was well aware of how difficult it is to brew a really nice cuppa with the syphon. Before I do any thing stupid with the gear, I decided to watch and follow youtube tutorials.

Most videos/online recipe told me the following recipe: Medium ground, 1:16 ratio, 90~95 C, and 45 sec. I followed this method and tried it many times But it didn't taste like the ones I usually get from my regular places. I couldn't find any aroma what so ever and the coffee tasted like nothing.

After asking some barista mates and spending sometime experimenting my brewing method (altering ground, brewing time, stirring method, and temperature), I've found my own recipe. Or rather, a recipe for the beans I've bought from a local roaster.

The popular opinion amongst my barista friends was 75-78C, 45 sec of brewing time, medium to semi fine ground with 1:15 ratio. I tried this method and it was much better than the one I tried before. I could smell the aroma, but it still lacked some taste. I decided to have a small experiment. I raised temperature by 1 c, every time I brewed a cuppa out of syphon. I decided to stick to medium-fine ground. Also, I adopted different stirring method, and brewing and resting time. And I finally discovered my own syphon brewing recipe.

tr:dl So here is my recipe:

Brewing temperature: 81C

Ground: Medium-fine ground (more close to medium side)

Brewing time: 45 seconds (burner-off time)/ 1 min 40 seconds (incl resting time)

Ratio: 1:15-16 ish (I use 13g of ground beans and 199~200g of water)

(Beans: Sidamo, Ethiopia - the beans are roasted from Atomic Coffee, New Zealand)

1) pre-heat water by using the kettle.

2) measure 13g of beans, but do not grind them yet.

3) measure 199~200g of water with a (drip) scale by pouring it straight in to the lower chamber of syphon.

4) start boiling water with the upper chamber tightly sealed to the lower chamber. Set digital thermometer to 81C.

5) grind the beans while the water rising up

6) when the water is moved up and the level is stabilised in the upper chamber, try to stabilise the water temperature to 81C. You can do following actions:

a) if water is below 81C - close the upper chamber with the lead.

b) if water is above 81C - start stirring water with the stirring stick to drop the temperature.

7) Once the temperature hits 81C and stays like that for 10 seconds, pour the ground into the chamber.

8) Stir the ground-water mix in an M-motion for 20 seconds. And let it brew for another 20 seconds.

9) stir gently for 5 seconds, preferably in a circular motion. then turn your heating device.

10) let it rest for about 40 seconds

11) enjoy your cuppa!!!

I personally find the last 40 odd seconds of rest very important. I tried to skip this part few times in the past and it kinda lost the aroma/sweetness of coffee. I suspect that by letting the lower chamber sucking the air through the post-brewed ground beans in the upper chamber kinda helps the coffee to capture the aroma and the distinct character. I can't definitely prove it scientifically, but I definitely noticed the difference.

Feel free to try my method. It may/may not come out in a way you like. Also, please let me know if you have your own brewing method. I would love to try it :)
